sentences.text: The holotype of Unenlagia comahuensis is a partial skeleton from the Coniacian age that lacks a skull but includes vertebrae, ribs, a scapula, and leg bones.
Estimates of Unenlagia's size vary, with some suggesting a length of 3.5 meters and weight of 75 kg, while others suggest a length of just 2 meters.
The holotype of Unenlagia paynemili consists of a humerus and two pubic bones.
The name Unenlagia means 'half-bird' in Mapudungun, reflecting the describers' view of it as a link between birds and basal theropods.
It is hypothesized that non-avian theropods like Unenlagia could not lift their forelimbs above their backs.
A Unenlagia skeleton was discovered in the Sierra del Portezuelo in Neuquén province, Argentina, in 1996.
Fernando Novas and Pablo Puerta named and described the species Unenlagia comahuensis in 1997.
A second species, Unenlagia paynemili, was named and described in 2004 based on a skeleton found near Lago Barreales in 2002.
Research suggests the scapula of Unenlagia was likely located on the side of the ribcage rather than flat on top, similar to other theropods.
South American researchers argue that a laterally positioned scapula would cause the coracoid to protrude into the ribcage, which they find anatomically implausible.
In its original description, Unenlagia was considered a basal member of the Avialae, making it a sister taxon to birds.
Mark Norell and Peter Makovicky classified Unenlagia as a member of the Dromaeosauridae in 1999.
Unenlagia belongs to the bird-like dromaeosaurid subfamily Unenlagiinae and is closely related to Buitreraptor and Neuquenraptor.
In 2011, Novas and Federico Agnolín published a study placing the family Unenlagiidae within Avialae.

A 2019 cladogram by Hartman et al. places Unenlagia as a more derived member alongside Dakotaraptor, while a 2020 cladogram by Motta et al. shows that Unenlagia is more derived than traditional dromaeosaurids.
Unenlagia lived in Argentina approximately 90 million years ago during the Coniacian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
The genus Unenlagia existed from the Turonian to the Coniacian, approximately 93.9 to 85.7 million years ago.
The classification of Unenlagiinae is debated, with some studies placing the group within Avialae rather than Dromaeosauridae.
It is debated whether Unenlagia evolved from flying ancestors and became flightless, or if bird-like flight evolved independently multiple times.
